Policy improvement

Once you know a policy's values, a better policy is one step away: in every state, pick the action that looks best when you look one step ahead using those values. The new policy is guaranteed to be at least as good everywhere.

The gridworld from Lesson 30. The values are the random policy's values after $k$ sweeps of policy evaluation. The arrows show which actions the current policy uses. Click a cell to see its four action values.

Is the new policy better?

Left: the random policy's true values $v_\pi$. Right: the true values $v_{\pi'}$ of the policy shown above, found by running Lesson 30's evaluation to convergence. Green numbers show the gain.

The maths

The action value from Lesson 22 says how good it is to take action $a$ in $s$ and follow $\pi$ afterwards. With a model, it is one step of lookahead on $v_\pi$:

$$q_\pi(s, a) = \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\big[r + \gamma\, v_\pi(s')\big]$$

In the gridworld this is just $-1 + v_\pi(s')$ for the cell $s'$ the move lands on. The greedy policy picks the best of these in each state:

$$\pi'(s) = \arg\max_a q_\pi(s, a)$$

Ties can be shared: any split of probability among the best actions works. The grid above splits them evenly.

Policy improvement theorem. If $q_\pi(s, \pi'(s)) \ge v_\pi(s)$ for every $s$, then $v_{\pi'}(s) \ge v_\pi(s)$ for every $s$. The greedy policy meets the condition, because the maximum of the $q_\pi(s, a)$ is at least their $\pi$-weighted average, which is $v_\pi(s)$ (Lesson 23). Proof: keep using the condition at each next state.

$$\begin{aligned} v_\pi(s) &\le q_\pi(s, \pi'(s)) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1}) \mid S_t = s\big] \\ &\le \mathbb{E}_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma\, q_\pi(S_{t+1}, \pi'(S_{t+1})) \mid S_t = s\big] \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 v_\pi(S_{t+2}) \mid S_t = s\big] \\ &\le \cdots \le \mathbb{E}_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 R_{t+3} + \cdots \mid S_t = s\big] = v_{\pi'}(s) \end{aligned}$$

Following $\pi'$ for one step and then $\pi$ is no worse than $\pi$. Following $\pi'$ for two steps is no worse than one, and so on, until you are following $\pi'$ forever.

If greedy changes nothing, so $v_{\pi'} = v_\pi$, then $v_\pi(s) = \max_a q_\pi(s, a)$ for every $s$. That is the Bellman optimality equation from Lesson 29, so $\pi$ was already optimal.

The theorem is about greedy with respect to the true $v_\pi$ ($k = \infty$). Greedy with respect to a partly evaluated $v_k$ carries no guarantee, though here S&B Figure 4.1 shows it is already optimal by $k = 3$.
